# 211 — explainer (HIGH tier): consolidating `yield.garden` onto `www.defi.garden`

## Goal

The product was live on two domains. `www.yield.garden` returned **200** and served the whole app
plus the whole 2,154-page static estate — measured with `curl` at the start of this run, not
assumed. This change makes that host stop serving the product and start pointing at
`www.defi.garden` with a permanent redirect that preserves the path.

## The intuition, and the thing worth un-learning

The instinct is "duplicate content penalty — emergency." That is not what happens. Google does not
penalise the same site on two domains; it picks one URL as canonical and consolidates the rest onto
it. The real costs are quieter:

- it may pick the *wrong* origin for some queries,
- link and engagement signals split across two hosts instead of compounding on one,
- crawl budget is spent twice on an estate that regenerates daily.

Those are worth removing. They are not an emergency, and the item was scored 6.0 accordingly — the
lowest-scored thing in the backlog, picked because it was the only `READY` row.

The exposure was also already small, for reasons worth knowing before reading the diff:

1. **The static estate self-canonicalises correctly even when served from the wrong host.**
   `curl https://www.yield.garden/tokens/usdc` returns
   `<link rel="canonical" href="https://www.defi.garden/tokens/usdc">`. The generators bake absolute
   `www.defi.garden` URLs, so all 2,154 pages already told Google which origin wins.
2. **`robots.txt` and every sitemap served from that host already point at `www.defi.garden`**, so
   it submitted no URLs of its own.
3. **Traffic at stake: 26 impressions and 0 clicks in 16 months** (GSC, `yield.garden` property).

So this is hygiene on a low-traffic alias, with one genuinely dangerous failure mode (below).

## What changed, in reading order

### 1. `vercel.json` — one inserted object, at the top of `redirects`

```json
{
  "source": "/:path*",
  "has": [{ "type": "host", "value": "^(www\\.)?yield\\.garden$" }],
  "destination": "https://www.defi.garden/:path*",
  "permanent": true
}
```

Four decisions are packed into five lines:

- **`has: [{ type: "host" }]`** is what makes this safe at all. Without a host predicate, a
  `/:path*` redirect to an absolute URL is an infinite loop that takes the whole site down. The
  predicate is the difference between "consolidate an alias" and "site outage."
- **The regex is anchored — `^(www\.)?yield\.garden$`.** Vercel documents `has.value` as a regex but
  not whether it full-matches or substring-matches. Under full-match the anchors are redundant and
  harmless; under substring-match they are the only thing stopping `yield.garden.evil.com` from
  matching. Anchoring is the safer reading of an ambiguity this run could not resolve without
  deploying, so it was anchored. The test proves the anchors are load-bearing by unanchoring an
  in-memory copy and showing the lookalike host starts matching.
- **`/:path*` in both source and destination** preserves the path. A blanket redirect to the root
  would throw away exactly the deep links this item exists to consolidate. The query string is
  forwarded by Vercel automatically *because* the destination carries no query of its own — which is
  why the test asserts the destination contains no `?`.
- **Position 0, not appended.** Vercel redirects are first-match-wins. Appended after
  `/tokens/index → /tokens`, a request for `yield.garden/tokens/index` would have taken that
  same-host hop first and only reached the host rule on the following request. At position 0, every
  path on the aliased host is one hop — which is what the spec's "at most 2 hops" budget
  (apex→www, then host→origin) assumes.

### 2. `test_yield_garden_redirect.js` — new, offline, 22 assertions

The redirect cannot be executed locally: `dev-server.js` is a 72-line static file server that never
reads `vercel.json`, and a PR preview deploys on a `*.vercel.app` host where the predicate
deliberately does not match. So the guard asserts the *config*, and does it by executing rather than
eyeballing:

- compiles `has[0].value` with `new RegExp` and runs a real match table — `yield.garden` and
  `www.yield.garden` match; `defi.garden`, `www.defi.garden`, `myyield.garden`, `yield.gardenx`,
  `yield.garden.evil.com`, `notdefi.garden` do not;
- a **blast-radius scan** across `redirects`, `rewrites` and `headers` asserting no *other* rule has
  gained a `type: "host"` predicate, so a future change can't silently host-gate the real origin;
- four **self-defeat mutations** (unanchor the host, flip `permanent` to false, drop `:path*`, graft
  a second host predicate onto an unrelated rule) proving each corresponding check actually goes
  red. A check never shown to fail is not evidence of health.

### 3. `package.json` — one line

The new file appended to `test:serial`. That string is the repo's sole test registry
(`run-tests.js` parses it), and `test_test_registry.js` fails if a `test_*.js` on disk is missing
from it — the guard item 205 shipped after seven test files were found orphaned.

## The deviation: spec §Change item 2 was NOT built

The spec asked for a second, "belt-and-braces" change: a static
`<link rel="canonical" href="https://www.defi.garden/">` in `home.html`. **It was deliberately not
built, and the reason is inside the spec itself.** Its acceptance criteria also require
`test_canonical*.js` to pass *unmodified*, and `test_canonical.js:112` asserts:

> `'home.html must not contain a static canonical link — the router must be the only source'`

Those two criteria cannot both hold. Building leg 2 means deleting a shipped guard from item 011.

Item 011's underlying argument still stands and is the real reason, not the test: `home.html` is the
single file served for `/` **and** for every `?token=`/`?chain=`/`?pool=` URL. Any static canonical
it carries is therefore the *root* URL, and therefore wrong on thousands of parameterised URLs
during the raw-HTML pass — the exact "collapse thousands of distinct canonicals to root" outcome the
spec itself names as "far worse than the problem being fixed." `home.html:98-100` states the rule
that settles it: *a missing pre-render canonical is neutral, a wrong one is actively harmful.*

And leg 2 has no job left once leg 1 lands. Its stated purpose was the single GSC
`Duplicate without user-selected canonical` page on the `yield.garden` property; a 301 means that
host serves no HTML at all, so there is no page left to carry a tag.

Recorded as an executable fact, not a comment: the new test's guard 6 asserts `home.html` still has
no static canonical, so a later run that "completes" 211 turns two tests red and finds the reason
one grep away.

## Risk

**HIGH.** `vercel.json` is named explicitly on NORTH_STAR's HIGH list (config/infra). The diff is six
lines; the blast radius is not — a host predicate that matched the wrong domain would be a
site-wide outage rather than a degraded page. It is **not** on the NEVER list: nothing is deleted or
de-indexed, traffic is consolidated *onto* the canonical origin, which is the opposite of
de-indexing.

The honest limitation: the redirect's first live proof is production, after merge. Item 212's round
4 is the precedent for why that is worth stating — a `vercel.json` that was valid JSON, semantically
correct and green on every local gate was still rejected by Vercel's own schema at deploy time.
Post-merge `curl` results are appended to `specs/211-notes.md`.

Revert rule, unchanged from the spec: if any `www.defi.garden` route regresses, revert immediately.

## Quiz

1. Why would this same redirect, written *without* the `has` host predicate, take the entire site
   down rather than merely misbehave?
2. The destination is `https://www.defi.garden/:path*` with no `?` in it. Why is adding the query
   string by hand the wrong move, and what would break if you did?
3. Spec 211 contains two acceptance criteria that cannot both be satisfied. Name them, and explain
   which one this build honoured and why that choice is not just the easier one.
4. The new redirect was inserted at index 0 rather than appended. Give the concrete request that
   behaves differently between those two placements, and say how.
5. The host regex is anchored even though it may well be redundant. What specific undesirable host
   would match if the anchors were dropped, and which part of the test proves the anchors are doing
   real work?
